newsitem.title: USA: Amazon.com: an Internet commerce pioneer.
newsitem.headline: Amazon.com: an Internet commerce pioneer.

text.p: There is nothing quite like wandering into a bookstore in the middle of a sleepless night, finding seven titles from that obscure but wonderful science fiction writer whose books are rarely found on bookstore shelves, and buying them for delivery in two days.
You can do that at Amazon.com, an online bookseller doing business out of its Internet Web site, http://www.amazon.com.

Amazon.com, with its selection of 1.1 million books, many priced at a discount, provides something book buyers can't get at a bookstore in the physical world -- the ability to buy almost any book in print in the English language, any time, cheaply.
And that, say Amazon.com's founder and several electronic commerce experts, is why it succeeds.

"You've got to offer something, some kind of service, that simply cannot be had any other way," said founder and President Jeff Bezos, who started Amazon.com in 1994 and opened its cyberspace doors 15 months ago.

"That is because Internet technology is immature -- you know -- your modem is slow, your PC crashes on you in the middle of a transaction," Bezos said. To make it worth shopping online with all the annoying aspects of the Internet medium, "You have to offer a very high value proposition."
Amazon.com has done that, or at least it convinces thousands of people each day to buy books, allowing it to grow its revenues 34 percent a month -- some 3,000 percent a year.

When electronic commerce experts talk about successful endeavours, Amazon.com is always on their list of the top three, along with Virtual Vineyards and Software.com (http://www.virtualvin.com and http://www.software.com).
"Certainly in the case of consumer retailing, Amazon.com is among the most successful," said Michael Taylor, Arthur D. Little Inc.'s electronic commerce chief consultant.

Isabel Georgeaux, a manager of Arthur D. Little's information technology group, said Amazon.com's yearly sales -- estimated at $17 million -- appear to be the highest among the handful of Web-based consumer retailers considered the pioneers of eletronic commerce.
Bezos himself will not divulge annual sales or profits.

Bezos, a computer programmer at heart, and his staff of programmers and book editors developed database software that allows visitors to the Amazon.com Internet site to search for books by author, subject or title and place an order with a credit card.
The software simultaneously places an order with the publisher to get the book to Amazon.com's Washington state warehouse overnight, and Amazon.com then ships it out to the shopper the next day.

Its Internet store front has allowed Amazon.com to do things book stores in the physical world can't do -- such as offer visitors the opportunity to "chat" with other readers with similar interests on electronic bulletin boards or e-mail the author or get notified of new books published in a given area. This "Eyes" service lets Amazon.com visitors register subjects or authors they want to learn about and get e-mailed every time a new title is published in that subject.

The biggest distinction Amazon.con can offer is five times as many books as the largest book store in the physical world carries. It can offer five times what Barnes & Noble Inc.'s largest superstore carries, Bezos said, because it does not have to store them in expensive real estate.
It also can discount prices, which it does on the top selling 300,000 books distributed by wholesalers, because it has lower overhead costs then a book store with expensive retail real estate.
Unfortunately for Amazon.com, much of its success comes from the nature of selling books.
That is unfortunate because after 15 months of phenomenal unrivaled success, Amazon is starting to have competition from other online booksellers.

Bezos knows that books have unique features that make selling books very suitable for online selling. Indeed, he decided to be an electronic commerce enterpreneur first and chose books only after studying 20 possible types of products.

"We chose books very carefully as the first best product to sell on the Web," Bezos said. "There are 1.5 million English language books and there are three million books in print worldwide. That makes books totally unusual in this respect, no other product category has this many products," he said. The sheer volume of titles in the world makes it a very difficult real estate problem of how to offer a lot of books.
Music and computer software and parts are also suitable for online selling for the same reason.

"Two things become important when you have a huge number of products, like books. Computers become extremely valuable because of searching and organising capabilities and secondly, you can build an authoritative selection. You could never have a bookstore with 1.1 million titles," Bezos said.

But so successful is Amazon.com that recently others have launched Internet based booksellers and also are succeeding. Moreover, two book wholesalers have developed software to encourage small booksellers to become online sellers.

"Cyber-bookstores are popping up all over the place," said Michael Shatzkin, president of The Idea Logical Co., consultants on electronic commerce and publishing. "Selling books is the second largest electronic commerce product emerging on the Web," he said.

"Shopping for books has historically been a needle-in-a- haystack problem and that is exactly the kind of thing the Internet is best equipped to handle. You can have a database of any size and search engines and so the issue for consumers -- to find the book the consumer wants, is one that can be searched for if the right information is loaded onto the database," Shatzkin said.
He said the two largest wholesalers of books in the United States, Ingram Book Co. and Baker & Taylor Inc., have each recently developed software to help small booksellers start selling online.
Also, a more equal rival to Amazon.com has opened shop, called "BookServe" (http://www.bookserve.com) started by two sons of a former Ingram chief executive.

"So (the) likelihood is that Amazon.com is going to find its franchize very difficult to hold on to because its advantage of being able to offer all 1.1 million books in print, pretty much anyone can do now," he said.
"The problem with the Web is it is very hard to hold an advantage for more than a few days," Shatzkin said, exagerrating perhaps by saying days.
